1:
The chapter opens by looking back, and Henry takes the first verse as a note on the genealogies just finished: they were gathered out of the books of the kings of Israel and Judah — not a canonical book but a civil record, authentic in the way a king's registers are with us. Gill adds a caution about what the preceding chapters actually contain, since two tribes are not reckoned there at all and the rest only in part; the exact account existed, but this book does not reproduce it whole.

Delitzsch spends his comment on how the sentence should be divided. The Greek and Latin versions attach the words about Judah to what precedes, producing a book of the kings of Israel and Judah, and then handle the remainder arbitrarily. He rejects that, and rejects with it the argument that Israel here means only the northern tribes because it stands over against Judah: the shorter title is cited elsewhere, and is admitted by the very scholar who presses the argument to name the same work as the longer titles do, so nothing can be built on the abbreviation.

The captivity is mentioned almost in passing, and Henry will not let it pass. Let that judgment never be forgotten, he says, but be remembered as a warning to those who come after; and when we speak of any calamity that has befallen us it is good to add that it was for our transgression, so that God may be justified when he judges.

With the second verse the register proper begins. Gill identifies the first inhabitants as those who returned on the proclamation of Cyrus and took up their former possessions, or such as were allotted them. Wesley makes the same point about the land — cities once theirs, taken away for their sins and held meanwhile by others — and reads the name Israelites as deliberate: it belonged to the whole people before the unhappy division of the kingdoms and is restored to them now that they are one commonwealth again, so that the names and signs of that division might be blotted out. Henry reads the general name the same way and notices who is gathered under it: with Judah and Benjamin came many of Ephraim and Manasseh and the other tribes, some who had escaped southward earlier, some who met them in Babylon and shared in the release. Trouble, he observes, drives together those who have been at variance.

Clarke turns the verse into a description of the nation's structure. The four groups named here are the whole people as it had been ordered since the days of Joshua — priests, Levites, the common Israelites, and the Nethinim, the temple's servants, descended from the Gibeonites who obtained their lives by deceit and were given that work; Clarke supposes that others taken in war were added later, since the Gibeonites' successors could not have done all the drudgery the service required. Delitzsch, looking ahead, denies that the next verse is a heading for the list of the city's residents — a heading would have had to name the priests and Levites who fill most of what follows — and takes it instead as introducing the chapter as a whole, which unlike the parallel register covers only the former inhabitants of Jerusalem.
3:
Jerusalem had to be repopulated, and the witnesses read the list of tribes with that practical fact in view. Gill notes simply that Judah and Benjamin furnished the largest numbers both into the captivity and out of it. Clarke sees several tribes taking advantage of the proclamation to return and mingling with those to whom the city had previously belonged, and judges the mixture necessary: a place that size needed the people to fill it.

Ellicott compares the wording with the parallel register and finds the first clause identical word for word, while the clause naming Ephraim and Manasseh appears only here — and nothing further is said about those two tribes in the whole chapter. He refuses to treat that as invention. It shows rather that the chronicler used the ordinary freedom of a compiler working from a fuller document, one that covered the neighbouring townships as well as the capital; the capital alone is what he chose to extract.

The first name in the register raises the chapter's standing difficulty, since the same man appears in the parallel with a different line of descent. Gill observes that Uthai is called Athaiah there though his ancestors are differently reckoned, and traces the descent given here through Omri, Imri and Bani to Pharez and so to Judah. Delitzsch sets him among three chiefs representing the three principal families of Judah — those of Pharez, Shelah and Zerah — settles a written and read variant in the line, and then states the problem without softening it: Bani turns up elsewhere among the Merarites, neither he nor Uthai nor any ancestor named here appears in the earlier genealogies of Judah, and in the parallel not one of the five intervening names agrees.

Three of the witnesses offer ways through. Ellicott allows the equivalences that are plain — Uthai for Athaiah, Imri for Amariah, both common contractions — and argues from the length of the interval that neither list can be complete: far more than five or six links would be needed to reach from the age of the patriarchs to the years after the exile, so each compiler has simply selected different names from a longer roll that held both series. Wesley reaches a similar result by two other routes, the Hebrew habit of giving one man several names, and the passage of time: this register gives those who came up at the first return, while many in the parallel may have come later and settled in the room of these men or alongside them. Clarke presses the second of those reasons alone, noting that the list here runs close to those in the books of the return and holds the company that came with Zerubbabel, while the fuller parallel takes in those who followed after; the writer's object in this place was to record who came first.
5:
The three clans of Judah are named in turn, and the first of them raises a question of spelling that all three witnesses answer the same way. The word rendered Shilonites looks like a gentile name from Shiloh, the old Ephraimite centre; but the list is of Judah's descendants, and Ellicott points out that Judah's three sons gave their names to three great divisions — Pharez, Shelah and Zarah — the second of which was called the Shelanite. Gill reaches the same conclusion, allowing that the men might be descendants of someone named Shiloni but preferring the Shelanite reading, and citing the Targum, which renders it simply the tribe of Shelah.

Delitzsch works the point out in more detail. The derivation from the Ephraimite city will not do, since no connection between Judah's people and that place can be shown or is even likely, and the older commentators were right to restore the form used for Shelah's family elsewhere. He accounts for the error by the fuller spelling of the name, which drew the pointing after it, and finds his restoration confirmed by the form in the parallel register. Both he and Ellicott notice that the parallel puts Maaseiah where this list has Asaiah — a difference Ellicott reduces to nothing, since the two names say the same thing, that the Lord has wrought.

Over the third clan the two part company, and the question is what the number counts. Delitzsch takes the plural in their brethren to reach back over all three heads named in these verses, so that the six hundred and ninety are the remaining heads of the three Judahite families together; the pronoun cannot refer to Jeuel alone, he argues, because the head of a father's-house is not a collective. Ellicott reads the same plural as evidence that Jeuel is itself a clan, and infers from the parallel — which gives a separate figure for the sons of Perez — that the number here belongs to the Zarhites only, leaving the other two families uncounted. He notes besides that the parallel omits the Zarhites altogether, though the source behind both must have carried them, and that on this showing they were the more numerous in the city; the compiler has again used his own discretion about what to keep.

With Benjamin the list turns over and the divergences multiply. Gill identifies them as the Benjamites who went into exile with Judah and came back with them, along with such as had lived in the city before. Delitzsch counts four heads and observes how unevenly their pedigrees are given — three generations for the first and fourth, a father only for the second, father and grandfather for the third — then reports that of the four only Sallu reappears in the parallel, and there with different ancestors. Ellicott adds that the parallel carries Sallu's line four generations further back, and proposes reading one link in this chapter's chain as a separate name rather than as another forefather.
8:
Three more Benjamite houses close the tribal section. Gill names them — Ibneiah, Elah and Meshullam — notes that their ancestors are given here and that none of these men is mentioned anywhere else, and reads the total that follows as the count of Benjamites resident in the city, which greatly exceeded Judah's. Delitzsch guards the sense of the summary line: the men described as chief of the fathers are the heads named by name, not the brethren whose number has just been given.

Ellicott turns to the names themselves. Ibneiah and the Ibnijah standing at the end of the same verse are practically one name, both saying that the Lord builds — that is, gives offspring — and he compares the same idea in Assyrian naming. Ellicott treats this whole stretch as answering to the Benjamite section of the parallel, which makes each difference between them a difference of selection rather than of subject. He observes that the sons of Jeroham had lived in Jerusalem before the exile as well as after it, which makes this house one of the older ones in the city rather than a family newly settled, and he suspects that one name in the list should be read with a different opening letter, on the strength of the form it takes in the earlier chapter.

The figure is where the two registers visibly disagree, and it is that divergence Wesley takes up. This chapter gives nine hundred and fifty-six; the parallel gives nine hundred and twenty-eight. Wesley offers two explanations and does not choose between them: the other register may count only those whom the lot appointed to live in the city, to whom this one adds the men who offered themselves freely; or some of those first settled there had died, or moved away on some occasion since. Ellicott comes at the same discrepancy from the wording rather than the arithmetic. The parallel, having traced Sallu's ancestry through six degrees, continues with two names run together without a conjunction and then the smaller figure — a statement that looks quite unlike what stands here, though the missing conjunction may mean the two are not being counted as separate men at all.
10:
With the priests the register changes character, and Ellicott says why at once: the three names that head the section are not individuals but three of the twenty-four priestly courses David had instituted — the first, the second and the twenty-first of them. He notes that the parallel turns two of these into a father and son, which he takes for a copyist's mistake rather than a variant tradition — a scribe who read two course names as two men had already lost hold of the arrangement the register is recording. Delitzsch reads the names the same way, as classes of priests who had their dwelling in the city, and Gill says only what the verse says, that these were the priests who returned and settled there.

The man named next is given a title, and the title is what interests the witnesses. Gill traces his pedigree back through Hilkiah, Meshullam — the same man called Shallum elsewhere — Zadok and Meraioth to Ahitub, and identifies him with the Seraiah of the other records. Delitzsch makes the identification more precisely still, recognising him as the Azariah named in the earlier genealogy, grandfather of the Jehozadak who was carried away to Babylon.

Clarke presses on what ruler of the house of God actually means, and his answer removes a possible confusion. The high priest at this period was Jeshua the son of Jozadak; the man here was not he. The ruler of the house stood next in authority to the high priest, with what Clarke supposes was charge of the temple guard and command over the priests and Levites — the officer elsewhere called the second priest, the deputy who acted for his superior. The distinction matters for reading the register, since it means the list opens not with the chief priest of the restoration but with the official who ran the building. It also explains why the name is given a pedigree at all: Gill and Delitzsch both trace it back through the high-priestly line, so the deputy named here belonged to the family that had held the chief office before the exile, even though the office itself had passed to another branch on the return.
12:
Two more priestly houses follow, and both Gill and Ellicott notice that the pedigree of the first is shorter here than in the parallel. Gill lists the three links this chapter passes over between Jeroham and Pashur. Ellicott makes the same observation and draws the general conclusion he has been building through the chapter: the lines agree exactly apart from those omissions, so the difference is one more illustration of the compiler's freedom with the lists he was copying rather than evidence of a different family.

Ellicott then works through the second house name by name, and the result is an unusually complete reconciliation. The two forms of the head's name are variants of one word, and perhaps both are poor spellings of a third; one ancestor's name is very likely a mistake for the similar name standing in the parallel; two more are plainly two forms of a single name; and the remaining link is either an extra generation or a copyist's anticipation of the name that follows it. So read, the two lines are originally identical. He adds the detail that gives the section its shape: the courses to which these houses belonged were the fifth and the sixteenth, so that the register shows three entire priestly courses, two clans representing two others, and the temple's ruler all living in the city.

The number that closes the section is large enough to trouble two of the witnesses. Gill takes it plainly — these with the other priests made up the total, which exceeded the men of Judah and Benjamin in the city put together. Clarke is staggered rather than satisfied: a prodigious number of ecclesiastics, he says, to perform the service of a single temple, all of them able-bodied men, and that without counting the gatekeepers named further on.

Ellicott doubts the reading that produces the difficulty. He can hardly suppose that so many priestly clans lived in the holy city, and offers three ways of taking the words — that the phrase about heads of fathers' houses belongs to the previous verse and has slipped out of place; that it means no more than heads of single families here; or that it refers to further houses left unnamed, the total covering all the guilds and clans of the whole priestly section rather than the last one only. He prefers the third, and notes that the parallel's figure for the priests is smaller by some hundreds. On the closing description he is textual again, observing that the preposition rendered for is absent from the Hebrew and that a word may have dropped out. Wesley takes that same description and asks why it is there at all: the Hebrew calls them mighty men of valour, and Wesley reads it as a qualification for the office rather than a compliment, since a priest might meet real opposition in enforcing the censures on impure persons without exception and in keeping the sacred things secure.
14:
The third class comes up in order, and Gill marks the transition plainly: the Israelites and the priests have been given, and the Levites follow, beginning with Shemaiah and his line. Delitzsch sorts the men who follow by their Levitical descent — one a Merarite, another traced through Asaph and so a Gershonite, another through Jeduthun and Merarite again — and notices that the last of them lived out in the villages of the Netophathites rather than in the city. Gill adds the same detail from the other side, tracing Mattaniah through Micah and Zichri back to Asaph the singer of David's time, and passing on Hillerus's suggestion that the first name in the group is the same man who appears elsewhere under a slightly fuller form. Where the registers differ over a name he simply records it, noting that Obadiah is called Abda the son of Shammua in the other list.

Henry stands back from the names to ask what the section is evidence of, and his answer is about the temper of the returned people. Religion was in good posture immediately upon their coming back from Babylon, and he explains why: they had smarted for their former neglect of the ordinances and had then gone without them altogether, and both experiences made them forward in setting up the worship of God again. They began at the right end.

Two things strike Henry about how they went about it. The first is that they did not wait for a building. Before the house of the Lord was raised they had a plain movable tent and used it in the meantime — and he turns that into a rule, that those who cannot yet reach to a temple must not therefore be without a tabernacle, but be thankful for what they have and make the best of it. God's work should never be left undone for want of a place to do it in.

The second is that they did not invent the arrangement. In allotting their employments to priests and Levites they kept an eye on the model drawn up by David and by Samuel the seer: Samuel had sketched the scheme and laid its foundation while the ark was still in obscurity, and David completed it, both of them acting under direction from God. Or else, Henry allows, David had the matter in mind from his anointing and consulted Samuel about it in the midst of his troubles, the plan being formed between them. Either way the pattern had been little regarded for many ages, and what this register shows is a long interruption ended and the ancient landmarks observed again. Henry notices too that while most of these men lived in Jerusalem some remained in the villages, perhaps because there was not yet room for them in the city.
17:
The gatekeepers are named next, and Gill gives their office in a phrase — keepers of the gates of the tabernacle. Delitzsch works out how the duty was divided: each of the four men named, with his own brethren, watched one of the four sides and principal entrances, so that the four were heads of the divisions charged with the guard. He observes that the other register names only two of the four with a figure for their brethren, and gives no figure at all here, and concludes flatly that at this point the agreement between the two lists ends. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by the same route, and notes that one of the four names may have arisen out of the word for their brethren standing next to it.

What Ellicott makes of the names, though, governs the rest of the section. These are not individuals but families or guilds holding the temple gates by inheritance; all the Levitical functions seem to have descended in the same houses from father to son, much as civil offices did in the Roman empire, and tradition assigned the whole arrangement to David as the second founder of the national worship. His proof is that the same warder is spoken of in David's day and again after the exile, which no single man could span. He also moves the clause naming Shallum chief into the following verse, where it opens the description of Levitical duty that runs to the end of the section, and would render it that Shallum is chief to this day in the king's gate on the east — the eastern gate being the post of honour and the royal entry, whose old name would naturally survive into the restored temple.

Delitzsch presses that same clause in the opposite direction. He agrees it refers to Shallum rather than to all the doorkeepers, since the later verses set watches on every side; but he takes the words until now to presuppose that the temple was standing when the register was drawn up, which would date the source before the exile. He knows the objection — that the name king's gate could have survived into later times — and grants it in general, while insisting it can only be accepted if Shallum is first shown to have lived after the exile. Gill takes the plainer view that the porters were set in the same order after the captivity as before, and Clarke says only that this was the gate by which the kings of Judah went up. Ellicott, rendering the next clause as warders for the camps of the sons of Levi, finds the archaic wording deliberate: it carries the temple watch back to the wardership of the Mosaic sanctuary, where the Levites encamped on the four sides.

Shallum's own pedigree closes the passage, and it runs back to Korah. Gill and Ellicott both trace it through Kore to Ebiasaph, Ellicott noting that the longer name is a fuller form of Asaph and that the brethren of his father's house are simply his fellow Korahites. Delitzsch explains why the guarded building is called a tent: the ancient usage held, because God's house had once been one. He also follows the register back past the restoration to the ancestors who kept the entrance at the encampment of the Lord — the office reaching further than the men who held it. Clarke supplies what the keeping actually meant, citing Jarchi: to let no one but the priests approach while the sacred service was being performed.
20:
The register breaks off into the past, and the first man it reaches back to is Phinehas. Gill takes him for the son of Eleazar who served in the days of Moses and succeeded his father in the post, ruling over the host and over the Levites and their chiefs; he records that Kimchi mentions others who made this a different Levite of the same name, but the phrase in time past seems to him to settle it. Delitzsch sharpens the office rather than the identity: Phinehas held it not as high priest but while his father was high priest, in Joshua's day, on the same footing as Eleazar had held oversight of the keepers of the sanctuary under Aaron. He also declines to read the words about the Lord's presence as a statement of fact, since the grammar would require a connecting particle; they are a blessing pronounced on the man, and Delitzsch connects it with the covenant of peace given to him and his descendants.

The next name is harder, and the witnesses divide over which century it belongs to. Delitzsch notes that the verse stands unconnected to what precedes, with the usual conjunction missing, and that its contents are genuinely difficult. He identifies Zechariah with the firstborn of Meshelemiah who lived under David and drew the northern watch by lot, and then asks the question the identification raises — why this one man should be singled out at all. He can give no definite answer, and offers only a guess: that Zechariah may have held charge of the porters' service in the tabernacle before David's division into classes was carried through. Ellicott agrees on the period and says so more briskly, striking out the opening conjunction and observing that the verse turns abruptly back from the age of Moses to the age of David. Gill inclines the other way, allowing that some refer the name to David's time but preferring to place the man after the captivity, in an office that David had established and whose order was still being kept.

With the total the list resumes. Gill gives the two hundred and twelve as a figure fixed in David's days below which the number might not fall. Delitzsch reads the verse as returning to the enumeration broken off earlier, so that the excursions into the older history stand as a parenthesis — and then admits the difficulty that follows from it, since if the number counts the doorkeepers actually serving when the register was made, the clause crediting their appointment to David and Samuel does not sit easily beside it. Ellicott takes the figure the same way, as the count of warders at the period the chronicler's source describes, and notes without resolving it that the parallel register and the roll of the return both give smaller totals.
23:
The office was hereditary, and that is the first thing Gill draws from these verses: the men appointed in David's time to watch the gates were succeeded in the duty by their posterity. Wesley reads the oversight in the same way as dating from David, and both he and Ellicott stop over the phrase that follows, which calls the guarded building the house of the tabernacle. Ellicott gives the plain reason — the temple was not built in David's day — and renders the next words as for watches rather than by wards. Delitzsch explains the addition as a precaution against misunderstanding: without it, the house of the Lord might have been taken to mean Solomon's temple only, whereas the arrangement described belongs to the tent that preceded it. Wesley makes the same point with a further distinction, that the tabernacle meant here is not the tent David pitched for the ark.

The watch itself was set by the compass. Delitzsch has the keepers standing to the four quarters according to David's arrangement; Ellicott puts it as the warders standing to the four winds, on the four sides of the tent of meeting first and then, from Solomon's time, on the four sides of the temple's square enclosure. Gill adds a figure from another direction, citing the Targum for twenty-four wards in all.

The last of the three verses describes how the country Levites were worked into the rota, and here the witnesses simply fill out one another. Gill notes only that the villages were assigned them to live in. Ellicott explains the arrangement: the warders' families, like the singers', kept their farms in the villages round the city and came up for duty in weekly rotation. Delitzsch reads the seventh day as the sabbath of the week, on which each class in its turn took charge of the service, and takes those they came up to join as the chiefs resident in Jerusalem — the men the next verse calls the four mighty ones of the doorkeepers, for whom he cites a comparison with the temple captains of the Greek. Wesley describes the changeover from the incoming side: every seventh day the courses were exchanged, and those arriving stayed until the next sabbath, serving alongside the chief porters, who never left the place of worship at all.
26:
The four chief gatekeepers are set apart from the rest by the terms of their service, and Gill is precise about what the difference was. They stood over the whole body of two hundred and twelve, with one man set over them in his turn; and they were never rotated. They did not go out to the country villages as their brethren did, but remained on the spot, in office, superintending the others. Delitzsch adds what fell to them besides the watch itself: the chambers and the treasuries of the house of God were in their charge, which is reason enough for their posts being permanent ones.

Their lodging followed from the duty. Gill places them in chambers built against the outer wall of the house, near enough to be at hand for their office at any hour. Delitzsch gives the reason the verse gives, that they passed the night around the house because the care of it had been committed to them, and then draws attention to the clause that closes it. The key was in their keeping — the word carries that sense in other places too — so the unlocking of the doors every morning was theirs to do.

Ellicott reads the Hebrew of the opening clause as saying that these were in fixed position, or in trust — the four heroes of the warders — and he draws the same contrast Gill draws, between the chiefs of the guilds who lived in the temple and the body of their members, settled in the neighbouring villages and occupied with pastoral work. He also moves the clause about the chambers and treasuries forward into the next verse, taking the account of the warders to close with the words that call them the Levites, meaning the Levites in the fullest sense.

Taken together the verses describe a standing household rather than a rota: men who guarded the sanctuary, lived against its walls, held its stores and its treasure, and opened it at dawn. That is the force of distinguishing them from the brethren who came up for a week and went home again, and it explains why the register troubles to name them and to say that their office was a fixed one.
28:
The duties now divide, and the division follows the value of what was handled. Delitzsch takes the first group to have charge of the costly vessels — the golden cups for the libations and their like — which were fetched from the treasure-chamber only for the short time the service required them. They were brought out by number to the place where they were used, counted again, and carried back. Gill describes the same traffic from the priests' side: these were the vessels the priests used in sacrificing, which the Levites carried to them and returned afterwards to their proper places. Ellicott says outright what the counting was for. The gold and silver were tallied out of the store rooms and tallied back, so that it should be certain nothing had been taken — a precaution against theft written into the daily routine of the sanctuary rather than left to the honesty of those who handled it.

A second group had a standing charge rather than an intermittent one. Delitzsch sets them over the vessels in general and over the holy vessels used in the daily sacrificial service, and over the stores that service consumed — the fine flour, the wine, the oil and the incense for the meal and drink offerings, and the spicery kept for the holy perfumes. Ellicott marks the same distinction more briefly, as the care of the ordinary vessels, those in daily use. Gill adds the working detail, that these men delivered the things out as occasion arose and saw to it that they came back when their use was over.

Then a line is drawn that the Levites could not cross. The spices were in their keeping, but the compounding of the anointing oil was not theirs to do. Gill states the limit plainly, and Delitzsch identifies the preparation in question as the holy anointing oil made up from several spices, which is why it belonged to the priests. Clarke puts the same restriction at its full weight: none but the priests were permitted to make that ointment, and everyone else was forbidden it on pain of death.
31:
Two more charges are named, and both are kitchen work done for the altar. Delitzsch identifies the first man as the firstborn of the Korahite Shallum already mentioned among the gatekeepers, and says he was set in trust over the pan-baking for the meal offerings, whose preparation he was to oversee. He notices a deliberate contrast in the wording: this man is called one of the Levites, where the preceding verse had spoken of the sons of the priests, so the two spheres are being kept distinct even as the tasks run side by side. The word for what was baked in the pan occurs nowhere else, and Delitzsch can only compare the term for a sheet-iron pan. Ellicott renders the office in plain English as fixed charge over the making of the pancakes, and observes that the narrative has turned back from priestly duties to Levitical ones. Gill adds only the identification of the man's father.

The shewbread is the second charge, and here Gill supplies the detail. Twelve loaves were set out each week before the ark upon their table and the old ones taken away; the work of these Levites was to make that bread and have it ready week by week, though the setting of it on the table was not theirs but the priests' — a division of labour that survived into later practice, where Gill notes that one named family had the office under the second temple. Delitzsch assigns the duty to certain of the Kohathites and ties the phrase about their brethren back to the Korahite house just named, so that the two offices belong to kinsmen. He adds the requirement that made the work weekly: the bread had to be laid on the table fresh every sabbath.

The pattern of the two verses is the one already seen with the vessels and the spices: the Levites prepare and the priests present. What the register records in each case is a trust — a named man answerable for one particular thing — rather than a general assignment of labour, which is why individuals are named at all in a list otherwise built of houses and totals.
33:
The singers are reached last and given least space, which Delitzsch explains by the function of these two verses: they are subscriptions closing the Levitical section rather than fresh entries in it. Since the enumeration of the Levites living in Jerusalem had begun with the singer families, the first subscription names the singers again, and Ellicott agrees that the words point back to the men already treated rather than forward to anyone new. Gill fills in what their service was — others of the Levites were employed in singing, masters of the song, presiding in that part of the worship.

The description attached to them is obscure, and Delitzsch says so before working at it. The word rendered free means, in later Hebrew, let loose or set at liberty, and he adopts the sense Rashi and Kimchi had already given it: immune from other duties. On that reading the singers waited in the cells of the temple courts, released from every other business so that they could give themselves wholly to their own; and the clause about day and night states the reason rather than a literal round of hours, which Delitzsch warns should not be pressed.

Delitzsch notes that the arrangement is symmetrical: the section opened with the singer families and closes by naming them again, so that the subscription answers the heading and brackets everything standing between. That is his warrant for reading these lines as a closing formula rather than as a further entry, and for treating the whole stretch from the Levites' first appearance as a single block of the register.

The second subscription closes the whole list. Gill takes it to cover everyone named in the chapter so far, the chief fathers of the Levites who were chiefs throughout their generations. Ellicott gives a more literal rendering, that these are the heads of the Levitical houses according to their birth-rolls; and with the note that they dwelt at Jerusalem the register of the restored city comes to an end. What follows belongs to another subject altogether, and the chapter's last movement is a genealogy rather than a roll of residents.
35:
The chapter ends with a family tree that has already been given once, and the witnesses divide sharply over why. Henry states the facts without softening them: these verses are the very same as those in the earlier chapter, setting out the ancestors of Saul and the posterity of Jonathan, except that there they conclude the genealogy of Benjamin while here they introduce the story of Saul. He takes the repetition as he finds it — and then says what he suspects. If it is granted that the originals of these books contain some errors of the transcribers, he is tempted to think the repetition arose from a copyist's slip: having written the words about these men dwelling in Jerusalem, the scribe's eye caught the same words in the earlier chapter and he carried on with what followed there instead of what followed here, and when he saw his mistake was unwilling to spoil his page and let it stand. Henry closes with the lawyer's maxim that what is redundant does no harm.

Delitzsch reads the same repetition as deliberate and structural. The register is given again to join the history of the kingship that follows to the genealogies that precede it; it stands as the introduction to the account of Saul's death, which is itself the hinge on which the book turns to David. And he draws an argument from the differences between the two copies: the deviations show that this one was taken from a separate document, better preserved than the version in the earlier chapter, whose text had suffered considerably in transmission. What Henry treats as an accident to be excused, Delitzsch treats as evidence about sources.

The details attract the other witnesses. Gill points out that the name of Gibeon's father is supplied here where the earlier list left it out — one of the very differences Delitzsch builds on. Clarke finds a departure of another kind, this time by the translators: the word rendered wife is in the original the word for sister, though the ancient versions and the parallel passage all read wife, as do almost all the early printed and manuscript editions, only one of the great Polyglots preserving the alternative. Ellicott takes up the names themselves, hearing in one of them the divine title Rock, which he illustrates from other compounds built on it, and noting that two names in the list have been run together into one meaning that Baal is prince.
